## Learning Objective

Define, use, and interpret the following terms:

- Left censoring
- Right censoring
- Interval censoring
- Independent censoring


## Lesson

It is very common in medical research for the outcome to be the time
from some origin to some event.
Here are some examples:

- Time from diagnosis to death.
- Time from treatment onset to recovery.
- Time from treatment completion to disease progression.

When time-to-event is the outcome,
it's very common to have partial information about the outcome.
There are a few ways this information can be missing,
as described in the following subsections.

### Right Censoring

The most common version of partial information for time-to-event data
is "right censoring".
Right censoring occurs when you know the event happened after
some amount of time, but you don't know exactly when.
If $T$ is the time to event,
you know $T > t$, but not the exact value of $T$.
Right censoring is depicted in this figure:

```{r}
plot(x = NULL,
     ylab = "",
     xlab = "Time since [time origin] in [units]",
     xlim = c(0,3),
     ylim = c(0,2),
     yaxt = "n",
     main = "Right Censoring")
points(x = 0,
       y = 1,
       pch = "|")
segments(x0 = c(1  ,1  ,2  ,2  ),
         y0 = c(0.5,1.5,1.5,0.5),
         x1 = c(1  ,2  ,2  ,1  ),
         y1 = c(1.5,1.5,0.5,0.5))
text(x = 1.5,
     y = 1.75,
     labels = "Window of observation")
points(x = 2.5,
       y = 1,
       pch = 4)
segments(x0 = 0,
         y0 = 1,
         x1 = 2.5,
         y1 = 1)
```

Here are a couple examples of right censoring:

- You recruit people into a study and follow them for five years.
If a participant doesn't have the event before the five years are up,
you know their event occurred after the study ended,
but you don't know exactly when.
- If someone in your study moves away and ceases participating,
you know their event occurred after this rupture,
but not exactly when.


### Left Censoring

As you might be able to guess,
left censoring occurs when you know the event occurred before some time,
but not exactly when.
If $T$ is the time to the event,
you know $T < t$, but not the exact value of $T$.
Left censoring is depicted in the following figure:

```{r}
plot(x = NULL,
     ylab = "",
     xlab = "Time since [time origin] in [units]",
     xlim = c(0,3),
     ylim = c(0,2),
     yaxt = "n",
     main = "Left Censoring")
points(x = 0,
       y = 1,
       pch = "|")
segments(x0 = c(1  ,1  ,2  ,2  ),
         y0 = c(0.5,1.5,1.5,0.5),
         x1 = c(1  ,2  ,2  ,1  ),
         y1 = c(1.5,1.5,0.5,0.5))
text(x = 1.5,
     y = 1.75,
     labels = "Window of observation")
points(x = 0.5,
       y = 1,
       pch = 4)
segments(x0 = 0,
         y0 = 1,
         x1 = 0.5,
         y1 = 1)
```

An example of left censoring is when a patient enters your clinic
with a rash,
but they don't remember exactly when it started.
You know the rash appeared before their clinic visit,
but not exactly when.

### Interval Censoring

Interval censoring occurs when you know the event
happened between two time-points,
but not exactly when.
If $T$ is the time to the event,
interval censoring occurs when you know $t_1 < T < t_2$,
but not the exact value of $T$.
Interval censoring is depicted in the following figure:

```{r}
plot(x = NULL,
     ylab = "",
     xlab = "Time since [time origin] in [units]",
     xlim = c(0,3),
     ylim = c(0,2),
     yaxt = "n",
     main = "Interval Censoring")
points(x = 0,
       y = 1,
       pch = "|")
segments(x0 = c(0.5,0.5,1  ,1  ),
         y0 = c(0.5,1.5,1.5,0.5),
         x1 = c(0.5,1  ,1  ,0.5),
         y1 = c(1.5,1.5,0.5,0.5))
text(x = 0.75,
     y = 1.75,
     labels = "Window of observation")
segments(x0 = c(2  ,2  ,2.5,2.5),
         y0 = c(0.5,1.5,1.5,0.5),
         x1 = c(2  ,2.5,2.5,2  ),
         y1 = c(1.5,1.5,0.5,0.5))
text(x = 2.25,
     y = 1.75,
     labels = "Window of observation")
points(x = 1.5,
       y = 1,
       pch = 4)
segments(x0 = 0,
         y0 = 1,
         x1 = 1.5,
         y1 = 1)
```

Interval censoring might happen if you check in with participant in a study
at regular intervals.
If someone has not had the event by check-in \#3,
but they have had the event by check-in \#4,
you know the event occurred between those two time-points.

### No Censoring

Just for completeness,
the following figure depicts no censoring:

```{r}
plot(x = NULL,
     ylab = "",
     xlab = "Time since [time origin] in [units]",
     xlim = c(0,3),
     ylim = c(0,2),
     yaxt = "n",
     main = "No Censoring")
points(x = 0,
       y = 1,
       pch = "|")
segments(x0 = c(1  ,1  ,2  ,2  ),
         y0 = c(0.5,1.5,1.5,0.5),
         x1 = c(1  ,2  ,2  ,1  ),
         y1 = c(1.5,1.5,0.5,0.5))
text(x = 1.5,
     y = 1.75,
     labels = "Window of observation")
points(x = 1.5,
       y = 1,
       pch = 4)
segments(x0 = 0,
         y0 = 1,
         x1 = 1.5,
         y1 = 1)
```


### Independent Censoring

The following definition of independent censoring is taken from
page 38 of
[Survival Analysis: A Self-Learning Text (3rd ed.)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4419-6646-9),
by Kleinbaum and Klein (author's emphasis):

> Independent censoring essentially means that *within any subgroup of interest, the subjects who are censored at time t should be representative of all the subjects in that subgroup who remained at risk at time t with respect to their survival experience*.

Kleinbaum and Klein provide the following example:
Suppose you start a study at time 0 with 100 participants.
At the three year mark,
twenty participants have experienced the event.
This leaves 80 participants who have not experienced the event.

Suppose that 40 of the remaining participants are censored
at the three year mark,
and 40 continue with the study.
Independent censoring means that the distribution in times to event
should be the same among the 40 who were censored and the 40 who were not
censored.
So, if we check in again at the five year mark,
we would expect approximately the same number of events
among the 40 who were censored and the 40 who were not censored.

I hope you can see why independent censoring would be important
for analyzing time-to-event data.
We can only draw conclusions based on the values we observe.
If the people who remain in our study are fundamentally different
from the people who drop out,
we will draw conclusions that will only be true for the subset of people
who remained in the study.
If the people who remain in our study are essentially the same
as the people who drop out,
any conclusions based on the people who remain
will also apply to the people who dropped out.



## Problems

### Problem 1

Suppose my dad and I leave the house at the same time
to go for a run.
We run exactly the same distance,
but on different routes.
When I return to the house,
my dad has already returned home.
What kind of censoring has occurred for my dad's run time?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Left censoring.
I know he took less time than I did,
but I don't know exactly what time he finished his run.

:::
